item.content:encoded:
News / NewsBTC / Russia Sets November 22 Start for Exchange Crypto Trading, Subject to Approval

Russia Sets November 22 Start for Exchange Crypto Trading, Subject to Approval 3 min read

BTCUSD ETHUSD USDTUSD TL;DR: Russian exchanges may begin cryptocurrency trading from November 22 if their trading rules receive the Bank of Russia’s concurrence. The November 11 announcement sets operating requirements for venues. A separate asset-eligibility ordinance takes effect on November 17, so the two dates describe different regulatory steps. Russia has added another piece to its regulated crypto market framework, with a new ordinance setting the conditions under which exchanges can start trading digital currencies and digital rights. The Bank of Russia’s November 11 notice identifies November 22 as the earliest start under those rules, subject to the regulator agreeing to a venue’s trading arrangements. That condition matters. An effective date creates a legal opening; it does not show that every exchange is technically ready or that every prospective customer can place an order on the same morning. The exchange rulebook comes into focus Under the announcement, exchanges must register trading participants, maintain records of orders and transactions, and monitor trading. They also have to calculate specified prices and report trading information to the central bank using the procedures applied to other assets. These requirements address the organisation of a market: who participates, how activity is recorded and what the supervisor can inspect. The notice says the Ministry of Justice has registered the ordinance. It does not name a completed launch at a particular exchange or provide a forecast for trading volumes. Why November 17 is a different milestone The central bank’s November 6 asset-eligibility announcement set a November 17 effective date for an ordinance covering Bitcoin, Ether and USDT. That notice deals with which assets non-qualified investors may access and the conditions attached to their purchases. Non-qualified investors face an annual purchase ceiling of 300,000 rubles through a single intermediary. Qualified investors are not subject to that asset-list and purchase-limit restriction. The central bank says investors in both groups must pass the relevant test and familiarise themselves with crypto investment risks before transacting. Reading the announcements together avoids a misleading single-date headline. One concerns the eligible assets and investor conditions; the other concerns organised trading requirements. Neither removes the need to check when a particular intermediary actually makes a service available. Domestic permission and platform access differ A national regulatory opening can exist alongside changes at individual international exchanges. NewsBTC previously reported KuCoin’s withdrawal from Russia and Belarus, where affected users’ account notices determine their closure deadlines. Those developments should be assessed separately. A domestic venue’s permission does not change another company’s service terms, and an international exchange exit does not by itself tell us when a domestic alternative will be usable. For a trader, the practical questions include the identity of the intermediary, the assets it supports, how a purchase is funded and where holdings are kept. For an exchange, reliable records and price calculations become part of delivering a functioning service rather than merely announcing one. A new route does not measure new demand The market impact depends on participation after services open. An expanded route into Bitcoin could bring additional buyers, but it could also shift activity from one channel to another. Permission alone cannot distinguish those outcomes or establish how much fresh capital will arrive. There is a longer institutional backdrop. NewsBTC reported VTB’s conditional plans for direct crypto trading in December 2025. That historical proposal helps explain interest in domestic access, but it is not evidence that the bank has launched a service under the latest rules. The next meaningful evidence from Russia will be venue-specific launch notices, completed onboarding and observable trading activity. Until those arrive, November 22 is best understood as a conditional regulatory starting point. It is a material step toward an organised market, with implementation still determining what customers can actually do. written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

item.title: Would a Tesla–SpaceX Merger Be Bullish for Bitcoin? Careful What You Wish For
item.description: As speculation about a possible Tesla-SpaceX merger continues to bubble, cryptocurrency market observers are asking a crucial question: could it drain liquidity from Bitcoin CRYPTO:BTCUSD the way ...
item.content:encoded:
News / Benzinga / Would a Tesla–SpaceX Merger Be Bullish for Bitcoin? Careful What You Wish For

Would a Tesla–SpaceX Merger Be Bullish for Bitcoin? Careful What You Wish For 2 min read

BTCUSD SPCX TSLA BTCUSD As speculation about a possible Tesla-SpaceX merger continues to bubble, cryptocurrency market observers are asking a crucial question: could it drain liquidity from Bitcoin BTCUSD the way SpaceX’s SPCX IPO once did? A Merger Wouldn’t Trigger the Same Bitcoin Selling an IPO Did Benzinga reported in October how analyst Benjamin Cowen previously linked Bitcoin’s weakness ahead of SpaceX’s IPO to softness before Anthropic’s expected listing. His theory: investors were holding back capital for the next big offering. GSR’s Spencer Hallarn made a similar point to Reuters in June, saying "crypto is a funding currency for a lot of this" as investors weighed SpaceX’s planned $75 billion raise. A merger would work differently from an IPO, since RBC’s hypothetical all-stock model has Tesla TSLA shareholders simply swapping their shares for SpaceX shares and no cash required. With nothing to buy, there’s no reason for investors to sell Bitcoin to fund it. SpaceX and Tesla’s Combined Bitcoin Stash Isn’t the Risk It Looks Like Tesla’s latest quarterly filing confirms an independent committee is exploring a closer relationship with SpaceX, including a possible business combination, though the company cautions no deal is assured. Here’s what the two companies actually hold in Bitcoin: SpaceX: 18,712 BTC, unchanged since December 2025 Tesla: 11,509 BTC, also unchanged Combined: 30,221 BTC, worth $2.53 billion at Bitcoin’s September 30 close of $83,553.85, now worth roughly $2.16 billion, a $370 million decline That drop has nothing to do with a merger. It’s just Bitcoin’s price falling since the quarter closed. SpaceX spent $48.07 billion on property and equipment over the first nine months against $13.10 billion in operating cash flow, a gap that might suggest pressure to raise cash. But the company still held $89.86 billion in cash and securities at quarter-end, which undercuts any theory that capex spending alone would force SpaceX to sell its Bitcoin. Meanwhile, Polymarket currently prices a formal merger announcement at 54% by June 30, 2027, and 68% by year-end 2027. Could Huang Joining SpaceX Be Bullish for Bitcoin? Not Yet Elon Musk replied it “would be an honor" to a ZeroHedge post urging him to hire Jensen Huang , with Polymarket traders now pricing roughly 8% to 10% odds Huang joins SpaceX by year-end. If that hire happened, it could arguably be a modest bullish signal for Bitcoin specifically, since SpaceX already holds 18,712 BTC on its balance sheet and adding a high-profile AI leader could reinforce investor confidence in the company managing that treasury alongside its broader business. That theory didn’t play out Thursday, though as SpaceX shares rose about 2%, while Bitcoin fell roughly 3% alongside the broader AI and chip stock selloff. The split shows Bitcoin and SpaceX stock barely move each other right now, since the $2.2 billion crypto holding is a rounding error against a company worth well over $1.5 trillion. News / London Stock Exchange / REG - KR1 PLC - Update: Venice Infrastructure Operations

REG - KR1 PLC - Update: Venice Infrastructure Operations Refinitiv 3 min read

KR1 RNS Number : 7982C KR1 PLC 12 November 2026   KR1 plc Thursday, 12 November 2026 KR1 plc (“KR1” or the “Company”) Update: Venice Infrastructure Operations KR1 plc KR1 , a London Stock Exchange-listed onchain infrastructure company, is pleased to provide an update on its Venice (“VVV”) operations. Following its October Infrastructure Income & Holdings update, in which it reported holding 276,223 VVV valued at £5.77 million as at 30 September 2026, the Company has fully staked its current holding of 275,000 VVV, earning rewards in VVV at an indicative annualised staking rate of approximately 5.74% as at 11 November 2026. Based on available disclosures, the Company believes it is the largest publicly listed holder of VVV, with approximately 0.56% of the circulating supply, a position that reflects its conviction in the convergence of AI and crypto. Venice is a core holding within KR1’s Technology Infrastructure Strategy. In its Introducing Decentralised AI announcement on 14 May 2026, the Company disclosed an initial holding of 60,000 VVV and the commencement of staking operations. KR1 has since increased its position. Founded by renowned crypto entrepreneur Erik Voorhees, Venice provides access to frontier and open-source AI models for generating text, code, images, video and audio. The platform is designed around privacy, model choice and user control. Venice’s adoption continues to accelerate. Its October community update reported 5 million users, with the increase from 4 million taking 68 days. Daily inference volume exceeded one trillion tokens during October, compared with approximately 250 billion at the end of September. On 14 October, Venice’s Erik Voorhees reported annual revenue exceeding US$150 million. In July, Venice also announced a US$65 million Series A led by Dragonfly, at a stated US$1 billion valuation, to expand its consumer platform and API business. KR1 puts its Venice assets to productive use in two ways. First, the Company stakes VVV to generate infrastructure income in the form of newly issued VVV tokens. Reward rates vary, and standard VVV unstaking is subject to a seven-day cooldown. The second route uses DIEM, a token that holders can mint by locking staked VVV. KR1 acquired its DIEM separately and stakes it to access daily credits for AI inference on Venice. KR1 makes that inference capacity available to customers through third-party marketplaces. Venice’s buy-and-burn programme creates a further connection between commercial adoption and VVV. The platform allocates 5% of API credit purchases to buying VVV on the open market and permanently removing it from supply. New Pro, Pro+ and Max subscriptions trigger purchases and burns of US$2, US$5 and US$10, respectively, alongside discretionary burns. Venice reported that the value of VVV burned during October had exceeded US$1 million by 28 October. Revenue-funded purchases create demand for VVV, while burns reduce VVV supply relative to continuing issuance. This mechanism is separate from staking rewards and does not constitute a cash distribution to token holders. Keld van Schreven, Managing Director and Co-Founder of KR1 plc, commented: “We believe the convergence of AI and crypto could be one of the defining technology themes of the next decade. We put that conviction to work through our Venice operations, staking VVV to earn infrastructure income while retaining exposure to the platform’s growth. We can use those rewards to fund operations or reinvest them in productive assets. That reinvestment drives the KR1 flywheel, helping grow the earning capacity behind each KR1 equity share.” About KR1 plc KR1 plc owns and operates productive digital assets across the networks powering the convergence of AI and crypto. As the only dedicated onchain infrastructure company listed on the Main Market of the London Stock Exchange, KR1 draws on a decade of domain expertise to take a high-conviction, thesis-driven approach to its holdings, targeting a dual return profile: infrastructure income and capital appreciation.
